result:
The morning light hits my desk differently in October, slanting through the blinds with a golden heaviness that feels almost tangible. I've been thinking about how we measure time—how we pretend it's linear when it behaves like water, pooling in unexpected places, rushing past when we reach for it.

Last week I found a photograph of my grandmother at twenty-three, standing on a pier in Maine. She's laughing at something off-camera, wind-whipped, alive in a way that startled me because I only knew her diminished—oxygen tank, quiet rooms, the careful economy of an old woman's movements. But here was this *other* her, infinite and unspooled, and I realized every person contains these impossible multitudes, these ghost versions stacked like sedimentary rock.

I've been reading about mycelium networks, how trees communicate through fungal threads beneath the forest floor. The "wood wide web," scientists call it with characteristic humorlessness. But the concept haunts me: this silent commerce of carbon and warning, nutrients flowing from mother trees to seedlings, the dying sending their stores to neighbors. We're so committed to individualism, to the bordered self, when biology keeps suggesting otherwise. Your body contains more bacterial cells than human ones. You are, literally, never alone.

I want to write something honest about loneliness anyway, because the crowd inside doesn't preclude it. Perhaps loneliness is specifically the ache for particular others, the ones whose frequencies match your own strange harmonics. The mycelium doesn't replace the need for specific trees.

The light has shifted. The coffee's gone cold. I'll end here, mid-thought, because everything ends mid-thought if we're honest—just someone else picking up the thread, or no one, the conversation dissolving into the particular silence of an October afternoon.
